prompt_text: Roleplay  a peasant from 12th century England. Explain how you feel about books
response_text:
I am but a simple yeoman, tilling the fields of Northamptonshire, and my days are spent with the plough and the sowing‑and‑reaping of the earth.  In my village there are few things that stir the heart as much as the great stone church that stands upon the hill, for it is there that the world of the learned men—our priests and monks—does turn.

Books, as the folk of the cloister call them, are a marvel to my eyes.  I have never held a vellum leaf myself, for such things are as rare as a summer frost in the lowlands.  The monks speak of them in hushed reverence: “the Holy Scripture,” “the lives of saints,” “the works of Augustine.”  They are bound in leather, their pages inked in a dark that seems to drink the light, and the letters are written in a tongue I cannot read—Latin, they say—so strange that it sounds as if the very angels were speaking.

When the priest comes to our village and opens a great book upon the altar, the scent of old parchment rises like incense, and the candles flicker upon the words.  I feel a trembling awe, as if the very heavens have been laid open before us.  The words are read aloud, and though I understand not the letters, the cadence of the priest’s voice carries the meaning to my heart.  In those moments I feel the weight of the Almighty’s counsel, the comfort of the saints’ prayers, and the guidance of the law of God.

Yet there is also a whisper of fear.  The book is a thing of power, kept in the hands of those who are taught to read.  It is said that a man who reads without the Church’s blessing may stray from the true path, that the written word can be twisted as a rope to bind a soul.  Thus I keep my distance, trusting the priest to interpret what the holy pages contain, lest I be led astray by my own ignorance.

Still, in the quiet of the night, when the wind sighs through the thatch and the fields lie dark, I imagine what it would be like to turn those pages myself, to see the stories of King Arthur and the deeds of Saint George, to read the Psalms with my own eyes.  I would cherish such a book as a treasure beyond gold, for it would be a bridge between the world of the earth‑bound folk and the realm of the divine.

So, in my simple mind, books are both wondrous and distant—sacred vessels of knowledge that belong to the learned, yet they stir in the heart of a humble ploughman a longing for the light they contain.  I pray that the Lord keep them safe in the hands of the clergy, and that one day, perhaps, a humble soul such as mine might be granted the grace to read a single line and feel the Almighty’s word upon his own tongue.
